## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Call a function with arguments by position and by name, and use default values.
2. Read a function's arguments from its help page or with `args()`.
3. Install and load a package, and call a function with `package::function()`.
4. Read a CSV file with `read.csv()` and `readr::read_csv()`.
5. Check imported data and save results to a new CSV file.

## How functions take arguments

You have used many functions already. Today you will look at how they work. Here is `seq()`:

```{webr}
args(seq.default)
```

Each name before `=` is an **argument**. Values after `=` are **defaults**: R uses them if you do not give a value.

### By position or by name

You can give arguments in the order R expects, or by name in any order:

```{webr}
seq(0, 20, 5)                       # by position: from, to, by
seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5)      # by name: clearer
seq(to = 20, by = 5, from = 0)      # by name, any order
seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)           # mix: first two by position, then by name
```

A good habit: give the first one or two arguments by position, and the rest by name. `round(x, digits = 2)` is easier to read than `round(x, 2)`.

### Defaults

`round()` has a default of `digits = 0`. `mean()` has a default of `na.rm = FALSE`, which is why you had to write `na.rm = TRUE` on Day 3.

```{webr}
round(3.14159)              # uses the default digits = 0
round(3.14159, digits = 3)
```

### Nesting functions

The result of one function can be the input of another. R works from the inside out:

```{webr}
incomes <- c(120000, 450000, NA, 310000)
round(mean(incomes, na.rm = TRUE), digits = -3)   # round to the nearest thousand
```

Deeply nested code is hard to read. On Day 6 you will learn the pipe `|>`, which lets you write the same steps from left to right.

## Packages

A **package** is a collection of functions written by other R users. Thousands are free on CRAN, the main R package archive.

1. **Install** a package once on your computer: `install.packages("readr")`.
2. **Load** it in every session where you use it: `library(readr)`.

```{webr}
library(readr)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## In this browser
The packages each lesson needs are installed for you when the page loads. On your own computer, run `install.packages()` once per package.
:::

You can also call a function without loading its package, by writing `package::function()`. This makes it clear where a function comes from:

```{webr}
readr::parse_number("UGX 450,000")
```

## Reading a CSV file

A **CSV** (comma-separated values) file is a plain-text table. Excel, Kobo, ODK and most other tools can export one. It is the most common way to get data into R.

This lesson uses a small, made-up household survey in `data/household-survey.csv`.

### With base R: `read.csv()`

```{webr}
survey <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
head(survey)
str(survey)
```

### With readr: `read_csv()`

`read_csv()` from the readr package is faster on large files. It also reports the type it chose for each column, and it recognises dates automatically:

```{webr}
survey2 <- read_csv("data/household-survey.csv")
survey2
```

Notice that `interview_date` is a `date` column in `survey2` but a character column in `survey`. You will work with dates on Day 11.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
To export a sheet from Excel, choose **File > Save As** and pick **CSV UTF-8**. The `readxl` package can also read `.xlsx` files directly with `read_excel()`.
:::

### File paths

`"data/household-survey.csv"` is a **relative path**: R looks for a `data` folder inside its **working directory**. Check the working directory with `getwd()` and the files in it with `list.files()`:

```{webr}
getwd()
list.files("data")
```

If R says `cannot open file ... No such file or directory`, the path does not match where the file is. Check the spelling, the folder and the working directory. In RStudio, working inside an **R Project** sets the working directory for you.

## Checking imported data

Always check data after you import it. Ask four questions:

```{webr}
dim(survey)                                # 1. Did all the rows and columns arrive?
sapply(survey, class)                      # 2. Does each column have the right type?
colSums(is.na(survey))                     # 3. How many values are missing in each column?
table(survey$district)                     # 4. Do the categories look right?
```

## Saving results

Write a data frame to a new CSV file with `write.csv()` or `readr::write_csv()`:

```{webr}
large <- survey[survey$household_size >= 7, ]
write_csv(large, "large-households.csv")
file.exists("large-households.csv")
```

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Arguments by name

Create a sequence from 10 to 100 in steps of 15, giving **all three** arguments by name.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_seq
seq(from = ______, to = ______, by = ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex5_seq"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
`from` is where the sequence starts, `to` is where it stops and `by` is the step size.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex5_seq"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
seq(from = 10, to = 100, by = 15)
```
The sequence stops at 100 because the next value, 115, would go past `to`.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_seq
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, seq(10, 100, by = 15)))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 10, 25, 40, 55, 70, 85, 100.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get 7 values, from 10 to 100.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Read a CSV file

Read `data/household-survey.csv` into an object called `hh`, then count its rows.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_read
hh <- ______("data/household-survey.csv")
nrow(hh)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex5_read"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Use `read.csv()` or `read_csv()`. The path is already written for you.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex5_read"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
nrow(hh)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_read
#| check: true
if (!exists("hh") || !is.data.frame(hh)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Read the file into an object called hh.")
} else if (identical(as.integer(.result), 40L)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 40 households.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "hh exists. The last line should count its rows with nrow().")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Find missing values

How many values are missing in the `monthly_income_ugx` column?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_na
#| setup: true
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_na
sum(______(hh$monthly_income_ugx))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex5_na"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The function that tests for missing values gives `TRUE` for each one. `sum()` then counts them.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex5_na"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
sum(is.na(hh$monthly_income_ugx))
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_na
#| check: true
if (identical(as.integer(.result), 3L)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 3 missing incomes.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use is.na() inside sum().")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Nest functions

Calculate the average monthly income, ignoring missing values, and round it to the **nearest thousand** shillings.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_nest
#| setup: true
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_nest
round(mean(______, na.rm = TRUE), digits = ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex5_nest"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Negative values of `digits` round to the left of the decimal point. `digits = -1` rounds to the nearest 10, and `digits = -2` to the nearest 100.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex5_nest"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
round(mean(hh$monthly_income_ugx, na.rm = TRUE), digits = -3)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_nest
#| check: true
target <- round(mean(hh$monthly_income_ugx, na.rm = TRUE), digits = -3)
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, target))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: %s shillings.", format(target, big.mark = ",")))
} else if (is.na(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You got NA. Keep na.rm = TRUE inside mean().")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Round to the nearest thousand with digits = -3.")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Filter and count

How many households in **Gulu** have water (`has_water` is `"yes"`)?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_filter
#| setup: true
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_filter
gulu_water <- hh[______ & ______, ]
nrow(gulu_water)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex5_filter"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
You need two conditions joined by `&`: one on `hh$district` and one on `hh$has_water`. Both are text, so use quotes.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex5_filter"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
gulu_water <- hh[hh$district == "Gulu" & hh$has_water == "yes", ]
nrow(gulu_water)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5_filter
#| check: true
target <- sum(hh$district == "Gulu" & hh$has_water == "yes")
if (identical(as.integer(.result), as.integer(target))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: %d households.", target))
} else if (identical(as.integer(.result), sum(hh$district == "Gulu"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is every household in Gulu. Add the condition on has_water.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check both conditions and the spelling of \"Gulu\" and \"yes\".")
}
```

## Level 1 complete

You have finished the Beginner level. You can now run R code, store values, work with vectors and data frames, and read your own data. From Day 6 you will learn the tidyverse, the set of packages most R analysts use every day.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting `library()`.** `could not find function "read_csv"` usually means the package is not loaded.
- **Using `install.packages()` in every script.** Install once. Load with `library()` in every session.
- **The wrong working directory.** If R cannot find a file, check `getwd()` and the path.
- **Backslashes in Windows paths.** Write `"C:/data/file.csv"` or `"C:\\data\\file.csv"`, not `"C:\data\file.csv"`.
- **Not checking imported data.** A column of numbers read as text, or a missing row, will break later steps without a clear error.

## Summary

- Functions take arguments by position or by name. Defaults apply when you leave an argument out.
- `args()` and `?` show a function's arguments.
- Install a package once with `install.packages()`. Load it each session with `library()`. `pkg::fun()` calls a function without loading the package.
- Read CSV files with `read.csv()` or `readr::read_csv()`. Paths are relative to the working directory.
- Check imported data: rows and columns, types, missing values and categories.
- Save results with `write.csv()` or `readr::write_csv()`.

**Next:** Level 2 starts on Day 6 with data wrangling in dplyr.
